name: Pec / bicep implants

lead: Pectoral and bicep implants are solid silicone pieces placed under or around muscle to make it look bigger. Pectoral implants were first used for reconstruction and later for cosmetic chest contouring.
In looksmaxxing they sit under hardmaxxing, as a surgical alternative to training. Independent studies of cosmetic use in healthy men were not found.

paras: The implant is inserted into a surgically created pocket, typically beneath the pectoralis major, and adds volume and shape from underneath.

Reported risks include bleeding, infection, hematoma or seroma, shifting, asymmetry, numbness and scarring. Silicone devices are regulated as medical devices; much of the available description comes from surgeon marketing.

lead: Pectoral and bicep implants are solid silicone prostheses placed surgically beneath or around a muscle to make it look larger or more defined. Pectoral implants are the better documented of the two; they are described as prostheses for the reconstruction and aesthetic repair of a man's chest wall [1], and the use of the same technology for biceps is far less documented in the sources available.

Within looksmaxxing culture the procedure falls under hardmaxxing, the category of surgical or invasive methods, as a way to add muscle size that training has not produced. Published evidence is thin: no controlled study of cosmetic pectoral or bicep implants in healthy men was found, and much of the publicly available description comes from surgeon practice material rather than independent research [2].
infobox: Roughly 10 to 20 years without complication, per a surgeon-sourced summary [2]
Silicone materials cleared via FDA premarket notification, per Grokipedia [2]

paras: Unlike breast implants, which are filled with silicone gel or saline, pectoral implants are described as made of solid, medical-grade silicone elastomer [2]. They come in rectangular or anatomical shapes and a range of volumes, and are placed in a pocket beneath the pectoralis major muscle, commonly through an incision in the armpit [2].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia whose content may contain errors, states that the procedure was introduced around 1988 for reconstructive purposes such as pectus excavatum and Poland syndrome, and that a surgeon described its use for male chest contouring, including gynecomastia, in 1991 [2]. Wikipedia mentions the pectoral implant only briefly, in its breast implant article [1]. Bicep implants are not covered in either source.

General risks of implant surgery listed in the sources include bleeding, hematoma or seroma, infection, anesthesia reactions and wound-healing problems. Implant-specific problems described include shifting or displacement, asymmetry, capsular contracture (described as less common with solid implants), numbness and muscle spasm [2].

For silicone breast implants generally, Wikipedia reports complications such as rupture, capsular contracture and gel migration, and notes a 2021 US FDA boxed warning for those devices that acknowledges reports of systemic symptoms [1]. Those findings concern gel-filled breast implants and have not been shown to apply directly to solid pectoral implants.

The procedure appears in the looksmaxxing hardmaxxing category alongside other implant and body-contouring surgeries, as a route to muscle size that does not depend on training or testosterone. Published information about community discussion of it is limited.
